summary: Describes a Uniform Resource Name namespace for the Schema for Academia (SCHAC), used to name persistent resources defined by SCHAC participants. It is mainly for controlled vocabulary values for attributes in the SCHAC schema.

plainLanguage.summary: Universities need agreed names for things like kinds of students or courses. This sets up a naming scheme that stays the same over time, so different schools can use the same vocabulary.

subtitle: A persistent namespace for educational institution vocabulary values

tldr.problem: Universities in Europe and beyond need consistent, long-lasting identifiers for things like student types, course categories, and institutional roles so they can share information and avoid name collisions.
tldr.mechanism: TERENA, a networking organization, defines a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace called 'schac' that allows educational institutions to register vocabulary values in a hierarchical tree. Each value has a permanent name that will not change.
tldr.outcome: Institutions can confidently reference shared concepts like 'undergraduate' or 'postdoctoral researcher' by URN, knowing the name will remain stable even if the institution or registry moves.

today: RFC 6338 is Informational and remains active. The SCHAC URN namespace continues to be managed by TERENA under the European Committee for Academic Middleware (ECAM). The registry at https://urnreg.terena.org/ is maintained and used by educational institutions across Europe and internationally to register vocabulary values in LDAP directories and identity systems. No updates or obsoletions have been published.

sections.title: SCHAC and the Need for Shared Names
sections.content:
The Schema for Academia (SCHAC) is an international effort to define how educational institutions describe people, particularly for sharing data about students, staff, and researchers. It extends existing LDAP schemas like inetOrgPerson to cover concepts specific to higher education outside the United States. To describe someone's role, status, or attributes, SCHAC needs controlled vocabulary—agreed-upon names for concepts like 'full-time student' or 'exchange scholar'.

These vocabulary values must be stable and globally unique. A URN namespace provides this: it reserves a permanent, globally unique identifier space and ensures that names registered once will remain valid indefinitely, even if institutions reorganize or registries move. This document registers the urn:schac: namespace under IANA's URN framework and explains how to structure names within it.
sections.plainLanguage: Schools in many countries need to agree on what they call different kinds of students and staff. A URN is like a permanent registration: once you define 'urn:schac:userStatus:student', that name means the same thing everywhere, forever.

sections.title: Namespace Structure and Scope
sections.content:
The SCHAC URN namespace is hierarchical, using colon as a delimiter. A typical SCHAC URN looks like urn:schac:userStatus:int:student, where schac is the namespace, userStatus names the SCHAC attribute, and int indicates that the term is for international use (rather than country-specific). Below that, there may be country-specific subtrees (e.g., au for Australia, es for Spain) or organization-specific ones using an FQDN.

TERENA maintains the root registry and delegates authority to country coordinators and designated organizations. Each level of the tree guarantees uniqueness of names at that level, and each registrant is responsible for maintaining uniqueness in its branch. The namespace is global in scope: any institution or community can request registration, provided they go through the proper delegation chain.
sections.plainLanguage: The name is like a postal address: 'urn:schac' is the post office, 'userStatus' is the country, 'int' is the city, 'student' is the street. As you go deeper, you get more specific, and each level keeps track of its own names to prevent duplicates.

sections.title: How Registration Works
sections.content:
TERENA publishes all SCHAC URNs on a web registry at https://urnreg.terena.org/. When an institution or working group wants to define a new SCHAC vocabulary term, they request a URN from the appropriate subordinate naming authority. For example, a Spanish institution might request a term under urn:schac:personalUniqueID:es, the European academic space might use urn:schac:userStatus:eu, and global or international concepts use urn:schac:...:int.

All registry entries are published over HTTPS with certificates from a SCHAC-recognized certification authority. Names are case-sensitive and follow a syntax rule that excludes colon from the list of allowed characters except as a delimiter, ensuring that colon can only separate tokens in a valid URN. TERENA contacts registrants at least annually to confirm they wish to maintain authority over their branch; if there is no response, that branch reverts to TERENA.
sections.plainLanguage: To register a new term, you contact the right authority (your country, Europe, or the global group), they add your name to the public list on the web, and promise to keep the registration stable. If you stop responding, someone else takes over.

sections.title: Examples in Use
sections.content:
The RFC includes examples of real SCHAC URNs. urn:schac:personalUniqueID:es:DNI:9999999Z references a Spanish national identity number. urn:schac:userStatus:au:uq.edu.au:service:mail:receive:disabled identifies a status value at the University of Queensland (Australia) describing a disabled mail service. urn:schac:personalPosition:pl:umk.pl:programmer is a position type defined by a Polish institution.

These URNs can appear in LDAP directory entries, SAML assertions, and other identity systems to refer to standardized or institution-specific vocabulary values. Because they are URNs, applications can rely on them being persistent: a system built in 2025 that references urn:schac:userStatus:int:student will know that value means the same thing in 2035.
sections.plainLanguage: Real examples show how a university in Spain might say 'this person has ID type X', or how Australia might mark that a user's email is off, using the same names year after year.

references.text: Crocker, D. and P. Overell, "Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF", RFC 5234, January 2008.
